title: THE UNTOLD STORY OF JOAB
paragraphs:
THE UNTOLD STORY OF JOAB
The Most Dangerous Man in David’s Kingdom… and the Most Misunderstood
There are names in Scripture we celebrate.
And then there are names we quietly pass over because they make us uncomfortable.
Yet if you remove Joab from the biblical narrative, the kingdom of David may never have survived long enough for God's covenant promises to continue.
A man who repeatedly saved David's throne while simultaneously undermining David's authority.
The story of Joab is not the story of a villain.
Nor is it the story of a hero.
It is the terrifying story of what happens when extraordinary gifting outruns complete surrender.
And that is why his story still feels frighteningly familiar.
Because many believers today know exactly what it feels like to be useful to God while still carrying areas of the heart that have never fully bowed before Him.
Joab's story is not merely history.
The first time we meet Joab, he emerges from the shadows of David's rise to power.
Because throughout his life, Joab often acted more like his own father than God's son.
The irony is impossible to ignore.
And that tension would define his life.
To understand Joab, we must understand the world he lived in.
Mercy was often seen as weakness.
Family loyalty outweighed almost everything else.
When Joab's brother Asahel was killed by Abner during civil war (2 Samuel 2), something changed inside him.
"Why should I strike you to the ground?"
Abner did not want to kill Asahel.
But Asahel refused to stop pursuing him.
Eventually Abner killed him in self-defense.
Years later, when peace between David and Abner became possible, Joab saw his opportunity.
One of the most chilling verses in Scripture appears in 2 Samuel 3:27.
Joab approached Abner as though he wanted a private conversation.
Then Scripture says he struck him "under the fifth rib."
Referring to the abdomen or vital area.
He distanced himself from Joab's actions.
And herein lies one of the Bible's most uncomfortable realities.
A person can be extremely valuable and still be deeply dangerous.
A person can build God's kingdom externally while damaging lives internally.
Giftedness is never proof of godliness.
Influence is never proof of surrender.
Results are never proof of holiness.
Years later David's son Absalom launched a rebellion.
David fled Jerusalem barefoot and brokenhearted.
At the center of the chaos stood Joab.
The same man who had murdered Abner now became the shield protecting God's anointed king.
Scripture refuses to flatten human beings into simple categories.
The Bible is brutally honest about human complexity.
Joab was both faithful and flawed.
Just like many people sitting in churches today.
His mule passed beneath an oak tree.
His hair became entangled in the branches.
There he hung between heaven and earth.
David had issued a direct command.
"Deal gently with the young man Absalom."
In his mind, David's mercy had become weakness.
He drove three spears into Absalom's heart.
Absalom died hanging in the tree.
And yet another line had been crossed.
Joab once again achieved the right outcome through the wrong authority.
He protected David's throne while disobeying David's command.
And that raises an uncomfortable question.
Can success still be failure if it requires disobedience?
One reason Joab remains unforgettable is because he constantly exposes a temptation every serious believer faces.
The temptation to trust our judgment more than God's.
Joab often believed he understood what needed to happen.
Being right became more important than being submitted.
Eventually a person can become so accustomed to winning that they stop listening.
And that spiritual condition is deadly.
The Greek New Testament uses the word:
Literally carrying the idea of listening under authority.
But Scripture never portrays him as a man deeply yielded to God.
He often functioned from wisdom without submission.
And wisdom without submission eventually becomes pride wearing armor.
Near the end of David's life, Joab made one final disastrous decision.
When succession tensions erupted, he supported Adonijah instead of Solomon.
This was not merely a political mistake.
It revealed where his heart ultimately rested.
He had spent decades helping establish David's kingdom.
Yet when the kingdom's future arrived, he opposed God's chosen successor.
The man who had fought for the throne could not release his grip on it.
And many ministries, businesses, churches, and families have been damaged by the same spirit.
People who know how to build.
But do not know how to let go.
When judgment finally came, Joab fled to the altar.
He grasped its horns seeking mercy.
But a lifetime of unresolved rebellion had finally reached its conclusion.
The altar was never intended to become a hiding place for unrepentance.
And so Joab's story ended not in victory but in warning.
This is where Joab's story collides with ours.
Most people reading this are not murderers.
Most will never stand on battlefields.
But many know what it feels like to hold onto old wounds.
To trust personal wisdom over God's instruction.
To keep areas of the heart under self-management instead of divine authority.
The refusal to fully release the throne of the heart.
And then Jesus enters the story.
Where Joab grasped power, Jesus released it.
Where Joab defended himself, Jesus surrendered Himself.
Where Joab shed another man's blood, Jesus shed His own.
Where Joab sought a throne, Jesus carried a cross.
The Apostle Paul writes in Greek:
That is the path Joab never fully embraced.
And it remains the path every disciple must choose.
The Kingdom of God is not built merely by strength.
It is built through surrendered hearts.
God is not merely looking for capable hands.
He is searching for yielded hearts.
Maybe the most terrifying thing about Joab is not how different he was from us.
Maybe it is how similar he was.
Many believers have won battles while secretly carrying bitterness.
Served faithfully while refusing complete surrender.
Joab reminds us that God can use a person greatly while that person still has areas needing transformation.
But he also reminds us that usefulness is not the same thing as intimacy.
Impact is not the same thing as obedience.
Success is not the same thing as surrender.
Perhaps today the Holy Spirit is asking a difficult question.
What part of your heart still belongs to Joab?
The confidence in your own wisdom?
The area where you have achieved success but withheld surrender?
This may have hit harder than you expected.
It may become the conversation that changes everything.
The greatest battles are rarely fought on the battlefield—they are fought on the throne of the heart.
